report:
**Conclusion: yes—EMDR can alleviate PTSD symptoms**, and it is an evidence-based trauma-focused psychotherapy. The best-supported conclusion is that it reduces PTSD symptoms for many adults, but it is not clearly superior to other established trauma-focused therapies (such as prolonged exposure or cognitive processing therapy), and it will not work equally well for everyone.

A 2023 systematic review/meta-analysis of 18 studies (1,213 participants) found **small improvements** in PTSD, anxiety, and depression symptoms after EMDR, including at follow-up. This supports benefit, while also cautioning against overstating its average effect. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/37882423

Guidelines support its use. NICE recommends EMDR for adults with PTSD or clinically important symptoms more than three months after **non-combat-related** trauma; its rationale notes that most EMDR evidence came from this population and timeframe, with limited evidence at 1–3 months. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng116/chapter/Recommendations  
https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng116/chapter/Rationale-and-impact

The broader psychotherapy evidence is favorable but nuanced: a systematic review/network meta-analysis concluded that increased randomized-trial evidence justified confident first-line recommendations for trauma-focused CBT and EMDR, while identifying cognitive processing therapy, cognitive therapy, and prolonged exposure as preferred CBT-based options. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32284821/

Thus, your “yes” is well supported: EMDR is a reasonable evidence-based option, particularly when delivered by a trained clinician. Choice should also reflect trauma type, availability, patient preference, comorbidities, and tolerance for trauma-focused work.
